newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Foreign banks lead Singapore in agri/food finance.
newsitem.headline: Foreign banks lead Singapore in agri/food finance.

text.p: Foreign banks are ahead of the domestic banking sector in tapping the huge and rapidly expanding agricultural commodities and food finance sector in Southeast Asia, a Singaporean minister said late on Tuesday.

"Singapore banks and fund managers have not built-up the expertise nor the experience in funding food and agribusiness ventures," said Lim Hng Kiang, minister for national development at the opening of a conference on Food and Agribusiness in Southeast Asia organised by Dutch cooperative Rabobank.

Lim said he hoped the activities of banks such as Rabobank, which says it has the largest share of the agritrade finance market in the region, would spur local enterprises to move into the sector which has great potential.
He said although the share of agriculture in Southeast Asia's economies had declined, actual output had in fact increased significantly.

"Food production in Malaysia went up 183 percent between 1980 and 1993. In Indonesia, it increased by 62 percent and in Thailand 24 percent. By the end of this century, the Asian food market is estimated to be worth some US$450 billion a year."

Changing preferences towards processed food has stimulated the growth of food-processing companies and attracted a large flow of investments in Southeast Asia and Lim said he saw this trend continuing.

"There are tremendous opportunities in China, Myanmar (Burma), Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos. There is an urgent need in these economies to raise the sophistication and level of their agriculture production," he added.
Singapore itself has developed agro-technology parks to accommodate some 500 farms. These farms have an output of $450 million a year, Lim said.
The city-state is also setting up an Agribiotech Park to house companies involved in the manufacture of vaccines, diagnostic agents, seeds, seedlings and fermentation products.

Another major project is the development of aquaculture in the seas around Singapore's Southern Islands and the Riau Islands. Deep-sea floating net cages and modern technology will be used to breed fish.
This project aims to provide Singapore with 40 percent of its fish supplies, Lim said.
